location: Salem witch trials walking tour, Salem, MA
text:
Step-by-Step Audio Guided Tour: Salem witch trials walking tour, Salem, MA
Tour-Category: walking

Stop 1: The Witch House

Address: 310 Essex Street, Salem, MA 01970

Coordinates: 42.5201, -70.8955

Type/Specialty: Historic House Museum

Specific Examples: Original 17th-century architecture, period furnishings, interactive exhibits about witch trials.

Orientation: You are about to embark on a walking journey through Salem, MA. The Witch House, home to Judge Jonathan Corwin, one of the infamous judges of the trials, stands as a stark reminder of this tumultuous history, inviting you to explore the complex legacy that has shaped this town. Your first stop is The Witch House. From the Salem MBTA station, walk east on Washington Street, turn left onto Essex Street, and continue until you reach The Witch House. You may notice the charming historic buildings that line Essex Street. From the cracked brick sidewalk, the Witch House rises up in dark timber and sharp angles, its black clapboard exterior absorbing the shifting New England light.

The Witch House stands today as the only structure still standing in Salem with a direct link to the witchcraft trials of 1692. Inside these walls, the living pulse of Salem’s community during the late seventeenth century took its shape—marked by the patterns of daily life and the rituals of the hearth. In the spring and summer of 1692, Corwin became one of the judges presiding over the witchcraft hearings and prosecutions that would claim the lives of nineteen people by hanging and leave at least five to die in disease-ridden jails. Over two hundred neighbors from as far as Andover and Topsfield found themselves accused, as suspicion threaded through more than twenty-five communities. Decisions shaping the fates of many—some known, some now lost to the record—echoed through these rooms where Corwin and his family took their meals and tended their daily business. Unlike other homes in Salem, no accused witches ever lived here, but the rhythms of everyday life—candle making, garden tending, children’s footsteps on the stairs—were interrupted by the anxieties and rituals of the accusations outside.

Years later, in 1908, Frederick Richardson ran an antiques shop from within these rooms. When Richardson died, he left his business—and with it, the daily comings and goings of townsfolk seeking objects from Salem’s past—to A.. If you listen, the thud of a passing car outside mixes with the layered history inside, where each floorboard carries the weight of both the ordinary and the extraordinary moments that shaped Salem’s identity.

Directions: From The Witch House, stroll down Summer Street and enjoy the charming historic homes along the way. When you reach the intersection with Washington Street, continue straight, and you’ll soon spot the Salem Witch Museum on your right, distinguished by its striking facade and large outdoor sign. It is about a minute's walk away.

Stop 2: Salem Witch Museum

Address:

Coordinates: 42.5200, -70.8954

Type/Specialty: Museum

Specific Examples: Life-size witch trial dioramas, a comprehensive overview of the trials, and a gift shop.

Orientation: Stand before the broad, somber façade of the Salem Witch Museum. The heavy stonework and gothic arches, once the walls of a historic church, now shelter a space where the air holds a faint echo of incense and the shifting murmur of visitors. The entryway opens onto a hall where the weight of 1692 lingers—etched not only in memory, but in the very timbers overhead.

In this place, stories of the Salem witch trials are given faces and names. More than two hundred people fell under suspicion during those months. One such life was George Burroughs. In the fever of accusation, Burroughs was named as a witch and brought to trial. The story passed down in Salem is that, after hearings and prosecutions that left reputations in ruins and neighbors divided, Burroughs was hanged—one of those caught in the undertow of fear and vengeance. This execution became a fixed point in the narrative of the trials, marking the lengths to which the search for supposed evil could reach.

Another name bound to this chapter is Tituba, an enslaved woman in the household of Reverend Samuel Parris. Tituba was among the first accused, her story beginning in the shadows of suspicion and unfamiliar rites. Local tradition holds that her confession—whether forced or freely given—ignited the wildfire of accusations, marking the origin of the trials that would ripple through Salem and beyond. In this, Tituba’s story is not just of victimhood, but of the unpredictable power a single voice could wield in a community already on edge.

The museum’s walls carry the sound of narrated voices and the subtle creak of floorboards underfoot, connecting every visitor to the unresolved questions left in the wake of 1692. Just ahead, the tour traces how Salem has chosen to remember those who suffered in the shadow of these events.

Directions: Continue straight until you reach the intersection with Liberty Street; you'll see the Old Burying Point Cemetery on your left. Just beyond that, stroll over to the Salem Witch Trials Memorial, which will be on your right, nestled in a quiet area that honors those lost during the trials. It is about a minute's walk away.

Stop 3: The Salem Witch Trials Memorial

Address: 24 Liberty Street, Salem, MA 01970

Coordinates: 42.5199, -70.8951

Type/Specialty: Memorial

Specific Examples: Stone benches with victims' names, a reflective atmosphere, and surrounding gardens.

Orientation: As you stand at the entrance to the Salem Witch Trials Memorial, face the low stone wall and step forward until the granite benches come into view. The best vantage is along the main path, where the pale stone slabs project from the wall like quiet invitations, each inscribed with a name and a date.

The memorial offers stone and space rather than architecture or artifacts. Nearly 200 people were accused of witchcraft that year. For instance, sits among them. Accused in 1692, her refusal to confess sealed her fate. Every bench fixes a person to a date, refusing to let them dissolve into the fog of legend. The story of the memorial’s dedication is its own event. The benches, arranged as if waiting for their owners to return, invite visitors to see the cost of collective fear. The granite is cool to the touch, the edges sharp, the names plain. No ornament distracts from the record. The memorial’s restraint makes its message clear: here, at this site, the accused are not forgotten. As you move toward the Old Burying Point Cemetery, the stones mark the path from accusation to memory.

Directions: From The Salem Witch Trials Memorial, stroll down Liberty Street. As you walk, you'll pass by the historic buildings of Salem, immersing yourself in the atmosphere of the town. Continue on until you reach the entrance to Old Burying Point Cemetery, which is just a short walk ahead on your left. Enjoy the sense of history that surrounds you!

Stop 4: Old Burying Point Cemetery

Address: 29 Charter Street, Salem, MA 01970

Coordinates: 42.5197, -70.8953

Type/Specialty: Historic Cemetery

Specific Examples: Gravestones from the 17th century, notable burials such as Judge John Hathorne, and a somber atmosphere.

Orientation: Stand just inside the wrought iron gates, looking past the uneven rows of slate stones and lichen-flecked markers. Here, sheltered by mature trees and hemmed in by Salem’s busy Charter Street, you have the clearest view of the oldest stones and the prominent tombs that anchor this ground’s centuries-old presence.

On the far side of Salem’s modern storefronts and foot traffic, the Old Burying Point Cemetery presents a stark contrast to the pulse of the city. Established in 1637, it is one of the oldest maintained cemeteries in the United States. The air here is close and earthy; the crunch of gravel underfoot is broken by the occasional call of a crow or the rustle of wind through the branches overhead. This patch of ground has witnessed the city’s rhythms change countless times, from the earliest days of European settlement—when Salem, now a residential and tourist area, was an outpost on the North Shore of Greater Boston.

After the events of the trials, his life ended here, and his grave remains a fixed point in Salem’s landscape—a reminder that those who shaped the course of the trials did not vanish into history, but remained part of this city’s fabric. A few rows over is the impressive tomb of Simon Bradstreet, whose life stretched to the remarkable age of 94 before his death in Salem in 1697. Bradstreet’s story is one of endurance and witness: he lived through the entirety of Salem’s colonial transformation, from its earliest English settlement in 1626 through its upheavals and growth. His grave, substantial and carefully maintained, draws a line from the city’s founding days to the later turbulence that the rest of your tour explores.

Here, beneath your feet, lies the layered history of Salem—a city that served as one of two county seats for Essex County until 1999, and that still holds the remains of those whose decisions and endurance shaped its past.

This tour weaves together the stories of those affected by the Salem witch trials, illustrating the profound impact of fear and accusation on a community. It reminds us that the echoes of history continue to shape our understanding of justice and memory today. That's 4 stops in all.
